A Healer’s Kit has ten uses. As a Utilize action, you can expend one of its uses to stabilize an Unconscious creature that has 0 Hit Points without needing to make a Wisdom (Medicine) check.

As a Utilize action, you can set a Hunting Trap, which is a sawtooth steel ring that snaps shut when a creature steps on a pressure plate in the center. The trap is affixed by a heavy chain to an immobile object, such as a tree or a spike driven into the ground. A creature that steps on the plate must succeed on a DC 13 Dexterity saving throw or take 1d4 Piercing damage and have its Speed reduced to 0 until the start of its next turn. Thereafter, until the creature breaks free of the trap, its movement is limited by the length of the chain (typically 3 feet). A creature can use its action to make a DC 13 Strength (Athletics) check, freeing itself or another creature within its reach on a success. Each failed check deals [[/damage 1 type=piercing]] damage to the trapped creature.

As a Utilize action, you can use Manacles to bind an unwilling Small or Medium creature within 5 feet of yourself that has the &Reference[Grappled], &Reference[Incapacitated], or &Reference[Restrained] condition if you succeed on a DC 13 Dexterity (Sleight of Hand) check. While bound, a creature has Disadvantage on attack rolls, and the creature is Restrained if the Manacles are attached to a chain or hook that is fixed in place. Escaping the Manacles requires a successful DC 20 Dexterity (Sleight of Hand) check as an action. Bursting them requires a successful DC 25 Strength (Athletics) check as an action.

Each set of Manacles comes with a key. Without the key, a creature can use Thieves’ Tools to pick the Manacles’ lock with a successful [[/tool thief dex 15]] check.

Wondrous Item, Uncommon (Requires Attunement by a Spellcaster)

While this pearl is on your person, you can take a Magic action to regain one expended spell slot of level 3 or lower. Once you use the pearl, it can’t be used again until the next dawn.

Armor (Shield), Uncommon

While holding this Shield, you have Advantage on Initiative rolls and Wisdom (Perception) checks. The Shield is emblazoned with a symbol of an eye.

Rod, Uncommon

This iron rod has a button on one end. You can take a Utilize action to press the button, which causes the rod to become magically fixed in place. Until you or another creature takes a Utilize action to push the button again, the rod doesn’t move, even if it defies gravity. The rod can hold up to 8,000 pounds of weight. More weight causes the rod to deactivate and fall. A creature can take a Utilize action to make a DC 30 Strength (Athletics) check, moving the fixed rod up to 10 feet on a successful check.

Armor (Light)

Supple dark leather, close-fitted to a slight frame, the studs blackened so they won't catch the light. A bracer-guard is stitched to the left forearm, worn shiny where a bowstring has slapped it a few thousand times.

Someone let the seams out at the shoulders, badly, with the wrong colour thread — the work of a person mending their own kit by firelight rather than paying a leatherworker to do it properly.

Hand-rolled leaves scented with a swamp orchid that shouldn't make anything smell this good. An acquired taste that rich tables pay well to acquire.
A waxed linen bag of long golden tea tips, unbroken and fragrant. Merchant-grade luxury; brews the color of honey.
Pale silvery buds picked before dawn, by the smell of them. Featherlight; a whole bag weighs almost nothing and is worth its weight several times over.
Coarse dark leaves smoked over resin-wood, sealed in oilskin. Sharp, warming, and rare this far north.
A full bolt of deep-green silk, finer than anything the fen deserves. One end is water-stained, but a draper would still pay handsomely for the rest.
Three combs of yellowed whalebone carved with wave patterns, wrapped in oilcloth. Collector's pieces from some coastal workshop long closed.
An old oil painting of a bright river-country at high summer, thick with reeds and light. The frame is swamp-swollen but the canvas is untouched, as if someone kept it dry for years on purpose.

A large, genuinely masterful oil painting: three women at a garden table, faces turned just out of view, tea steaming. The signature has been scraped off. The work itself is worth a small fortune to the right buyer.
A black teacup chased with silver briars, so thin the candlelight glows through it. The inside of the rim is worn from years of use — always drunk from the same side.
A teacup of translucent bone porcelain rimmed in gold, painted with a ring of dancing figures that seem to move when the cup is turned. Museum-quality work; no maker's mark.
A teacup glazed in deep sea-glass green, its handle shaped as a curling wave. Held to the light, faint shapes drift in the glaze like things under water. Flawless, and very old.
A long, dark flight feather from a peryton's wing — glossy, edged in storm-gray, and faintly warm. Worth a fair price to an alchemist or collector.
A rolled tapestry panel, elven work: a hunt through silver birches, the thread still bright. Cut from a larger piece — cleanly, with very sharp shears.
A matched teapot, creamer, and three cups in blackened silver — heavy, old, and very fine under the tarnish. Three cups, not four.
The partial skeleton of a very young dragon — skull, wing-fingers, and a fan of ribs — cleaned, lacquered, and wired together for display. A collector or a wizard's college would bid on this.
